mainTopic: רבא's rulings on land disputes: when a claimant's words or behavior do or do not cost him his claim, and how חזקה competes with a שטר
overview: This amud is a series of short land cases, and רבא rules on each one. First, a claimant tells the person on his land that he is not the right opponent, since he never claimed to buy the land from him, and רבא agrees. Next, a claimant calls the seller a thief. The possessor says, 'You yourself told me to buy it,' and the claimant answers, 'The second buyer is easier for me to deal with than the first seller.' The גמרא challenges רבא for accepting this, since in a משנה only אדמון holds this view and חכמים disagree. It answers that even חכמים agree here, because signing a document is an action, while casual words count for less. In another case, a claimant asked to buy the land, and רבא accepts that people pay just to avoid a court case. Last, a holder says 'שני חזקה' really meant many years, and רבא accepts this. The גמרא limits that ruling to a holder who used the land for seven years, so that his חזקה was complete before the claimant's four-year-old שטר.

steps.title: The claimant says: you are not the one I must argue with
steps.stepSummary: The original owner tells the possessor that he admits the land was the owner's and was not bought from him directly, so the owner owes him no legal answer.
steps.simpleTranslation: [Do you admit] that this land is mine, and that you did not buy it from me? Go away. You are not the person I have to argue with in court.
steps.whatsHappening: We are joining a court case already in progress. The claimant answers the man on his land by saying, 'You never claimed to buy it from me, so you are not my opponent.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: The possessor did not say he bought the land from the claimant himself. Since he admits the land once belonged to the claimant, the claimant says the possessor cannot argue the case against him. Only someone with a direct claim against him is his proper opponent.

keyTerms.meaning: The opposing party in a court case, the one you must answer to

phrases.english: that this land is mine,
and you did not buy it from me?

phrases.aramaic: זִיל, לָאו בַּעַל דְּבָרִים דִּידִי אַתְּ.
phrases.english: Go, you are not my opposing party in court.

steps.triggerLanguage: זִיל, לָאו בַּעַל דְּבָרִים דִּידִי אַתְּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues a case that began before this section.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Someone who admits the land was the claimant's and did not buy it from him directly is not the claimant's proper opponent in court.

steps.title: רבא agrees with the claimant
steps.stepSummary: רבא rules that the claimant's argument is legally correct.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: He is telling him the correct law.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא decides the first case and says the claimant is right.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase 'דִּינָא קָאָמַר לֵיהּ' means the claimant's words are the actual law, not just a clever argument. So the possessor's claim of buying from a third person does not let him win against the original owner here.

keyTerms.meaning: He is telling him the correct law

phrases.english: Rava said: He is telling him the law.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rules on the claimant's argument from step 1.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The claimant's argument is accepted as correct law.

steps.title: A new case: the seller was a thief
steps.stepSummary: A possessor says he bought the land from someone else and used it for the years of חזקה. The claimant answers that the seller was a robber.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was a man who said to another: What do you want with this land? He answered: I bought it from so-and-so, and I used it for the years of חזקה. The first man said: So-and-so is a robber.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new court case. This step sets up the dispute that the next steps will argue about.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The possessor relies on two things: a purchase from a third person, and using the land for the years needed for חזקה. The claimant answers that the seller stole the land, so he never owned it and could not sell it.

keyTerms.meaning: The years of using land that show ownership

phrases.english: There was a certain man who said to another:
What do you want with this land?
He said to him: I bought it from so-and-so,
and I used it for the years of presumed ownership.
He said to him: So-and-so is a robber.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָהוּא דְּאָמַר לֵיהּ לְחַבְרֵיהּ: מַאי בָּעֵית בְּהַאי אַרְעָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new case, separate from the one decided in step 2.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Sets up the case: the possessor claims he bought from a third person, and the claimant says that person was a thief.

steps.title: The possessor: you yourself told me to buy it
steps.stepSummary: The possessor brings witnesses that the claimant advised him to buy the land from that seller.
steps.simpleTranslation: The possessor said: But I have witnesses that I came and asked your advice, and you told me, 'Go buy it!'
steps.whatsHappening: The possessor attacks the claimant's story. If the land was really stolen from you, why did you tell me to buy it?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Telling someone 'go buy it' looks like an admission that the seller really owned the land. So the possessor argues that the claimant cannot now call the seller a thief.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: וְהָא אִית לִי סָהֲדִי
phrases.english: He said to him: But I have witnesses
that I came and consulted with you,
and you said to me: 'Go buy it!'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the claimant's statement in step 3 that the seller was a robber.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claimant's statement that the seller was a thief.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Advising someone to buy from the seller looks like admitting the seller owned the land.

steps.title: The claimant: the second one is easier for me
steps.stepSummary: The claimant explains he advised the purchase because the buyer would be easier to deal with than the thief.
steps.simpleTranslation: The claimant said: The second one is easier for me to deal with; the first one is harder than him.
steps.whatsHappening: The claimant explains why his advice was not an admission. He wanted the land to reach someone he could argue with more easily.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'The second' is the buyer, and 'the first' is the thief who sold it. The claimant says his advice was a plan to get his land back from an easier opponent, not an agreement that the thief owned it.

keyTerms.meaning: The second one, meaning the buyer
Easy for me to deal with
The first one, meaning the seller

phrases.english: He said to him: The second is easy for me;
the first is harder than him.

steps.triggerLanguage: הַשֵּׁנִי נוֹחַ לִי; הָרִאשׁוֹן קָשֶׁה הֵימֶנּוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the possessor's challenge in step 4.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains the claimant's behavior with a different motive.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Advising the purchase means admitting the seller owned the land.
steps.terutzMaskana: The advice only shows he preferred to face the easier buyer, not that he gave up his claim.

steps.title: רבא accepts the 'easier for me' argument
steps.stepSummary: רבא rules that the claimant's explanation is legally correct.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: He is telling him the correct law.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא decides the second case in favor of the claimant.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because of רבא's ruling, the claimant does not lose his right to the land just because he advised the purchase. His explanation, 'the second is easier for me,' is accepted.
steps.whatToRemember: According to רבא, advising someone to buy a field does not cancel your own claim to it, because you can say 'the second is easier for me.'

phrases.english: Rava said: He is telling him the law.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rules on the exchange in steps 3–5.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The claim 'the second is easier for me' is accepted, so the claimant keeps his right to the land.

steps.title: Is רבא following אדמון?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whose opinion רבא follows, suggesting it is אדמון's.
steps.simpleTranslation: Whose opinion is this like? Is it like אדמון?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions רבא's ruling. It sets up a source to show that this reasoning belongs to אדמון.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The same words, 'the second is easier for me,' appear in a משנה as the opinion of אדמון. If רבא follows אדמון, he seems to be ruling like a single opinion against חכמים.

keyTerms.meaning: Like whom? Whose opinion is this?
אדמון, a judge in Jerusalem quoted in the משנה

phrases.english: Like whom? Like Admon?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the source of רבא's ruling in step 6.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which תנא's opinion רבא's ruling matches.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's ruling in step 6 that the claimant's 'the second is easier for me' explanation is valid law.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The 'easier for me' argument is אדמון's lone view in the משנה, and חכמים reject it. So רבא appears to rule against the majority.

steps.title: The משנה: אדמון versus חכמים
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a משנה. A man contests a field on whose sale document he signed as a witness. אדמון says he can still claim, but חכמים say he lost his right.
steps.simpleTranslation: As we learned in a משנה: If someone contests ownership of a field, and he himself signed as a witness on its sale document, אדמון says he can say, 'The second is easier for me; the first is harder than him.' חכמים say he lost his right.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings the source behind its question. It shows that the 'easier for me' argument is אדמון's, while חכמים reject it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Signing as a witness on the sale is like advising the purchase, since both seem to admit the seller owned the field. אדמון allows the claimant to explain himself, but חכמים say he gave up his claim. So רבא's ruling seems to match אדמון, the lone opinion.

keyTerms.meaning: As we learned in a משנה
Signed on it as a witness

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up 'the second' and 'the first.' 'The second' is the buyer now holding the field, and 'the first' is the seller.
steps.whyThisMatters: Usually the law follows חכמים over a single opinion, so if רבא follows אדמון his ruling looks problematic.

phrases.english: As we learned: One who contests ownership of a field
phrases.notes: This משנה is in מסכת כתובות.

phrases.english: and is signed on it as a witness –
phrases.notes: He signed the sale document of that very field, the one selling it to someone else.

phrases.english: Admon says: The second is easy for me;
the first is harder than him.
And the Sages say: He lost his right.

steps.triggerLanguage: דִּתְנַן: הָעוֹרֵר עַל הַשָּׂדֶה וְחָתוּם עָלֶיהָ בְּעֵד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the משנה behind the question in step 7.
steps.raayaObject: That רבא's ruling matches אדמון's opinion.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה in כתובות about a claimant who signed as a witness on the field's sale document.

steps.title: Even רבנן agree: an action differs from mere words
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says רבא's ruling can fit the חכמים too. In the משנה the claimant did an action by signing the sale document. In רבא's case he only spoke, and people often say things casually.
steps.simpleTranslation: You can even say רבא agrees with the חכמים. There, the man did an action by signing. Here it was only talk, and people often say things without meaning much by them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers its own question from step 7. רבא does not need to follow אדמון, because his case is different from the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The חכמים say the signer lost his claim because signing a sale document is a real action that shows the field belongs to someone else. In רבא's case the claimant only gave advice in words. Casual words are weaker than an action, so even the חכמים would let him keep his claim.

keyTerms.meaning: You can even say (the ruling fits this opinion too)

steps.whatToRemember: Signing a document is an action and can cost a person his claim. Casual talk is only words, and a person is not held to it so strongly.
steps.confusionAlert: This does not mean the חכמים changed their mind about the signer. Their ruling still stands. רבא's case is simply a different kind of case.

phrases.english: You may even say it follows the Rabbis
phrases.notes: The Rabbis here are the חכמים who argued with אדמון in the משנה from step 8.

phrases.english: There, he did an action for him;
phrases.notes: "There" means the משנה case, where he signed as a witness on the sale document.

phrases.english: but here it is only speech –
a person tends to say things casually.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the suggestion that רבא must follow אדמון by pointing out a difference between the משנה and רבא's case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבא's ruling seemed to match only אדמון's view, since the חכמים say the signer lost his claim.
steps.terutzMaskana: Even the חכמים agree with רבא, because his case has only words, not an action.

steps.title: A new case: the seller is called a robber
steps.stepSummary: A man challenges someone holding his land. The holder says he bought it from a certain person and used it for the years of חזקה. The claimant answers that the seller was a robber.
steps.simpleTranslation: A man said to another: Why are you on this land? He answered: I bought it from so-and-so and used it for the years of חזקה. The first man said: So-and-so is a robber!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new story about a land dispute. This step sets up the case for the next moves.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The holder makes a normal claim of ownership: he bought it and held it for the years of חזקה. The claimant says the seller stole the land from him, so the sale meant nothing.

keyTerms.meaning: The years (usually three) of use that set up proof of ownership

phrases.english: There was a certain person who said to another:
What are you doing with this land?
He said to him: I bought it from so-and-so,
and I used it for the years of חזקה.
He said to him: So-and-so is a robber!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new case about land ownership, also ruled on by רבא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Sets up the case: a buyer claims ownership through purchase and חזקה, and the claimant calls the seller a robber.

steps.title: The holder's witnesses: you asked me to sell it to you
steps.stepSummary: The holder says he has witnesses that the claimant came at night and asked to buy the land from him. That seems to show the claimant agreed the land was not his.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said: But I have witnesses that you came to me at night and said: Sell it to me!
steps.whatsHappening: The holder attacks the claimant's story. If the land was really yours, why did you ask to buy it from me?
steps.deeperAnalysis: A real owner would demand his land back for free. Asking to buy it looks like an admission that the holder owns it.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: וְהָא אִית לִי סָהֲדִי
phrases.english: He said to him: But I have witnesses
that you came at night,
and you said to me: Sell it to me!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the claimant's statement that the seller was a robber.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claimant's claim that the land is his and the seller stole it.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Asking to buy the land suggests the claimant admitted it belonged to the holder.

steps.title: The claimant: I wanted to buy my way out of a lawsuit
steps.stepSummary: The claimant explains he offered to buy the land only to avoid going to court.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said: I thought, let me pay to avoid a lawsuit.
steps.whatsHappening: The claimant defends himself against the witnesses. He says his offer was not an admission.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He did not ask to buy because the land was the holder's. He wanted to save himself the trouble and cost of a court case to get back his own land.

keyTerms.meaning: I said, I thought to myself

phrases.english: He said to him: I thought, I will buy off my lawsuit.
phrases.notes: He means he would rather pay than go through a court case to get his land back.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the holder's challenge from the witnesses.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explaining the reason behind the action
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Asking to buy the land meant the claimant admitted it was not his.
steps.terutzMaskana: He asked to buy only to avoid a court case, not because he gave up his ownership.

steps.title: רבא: people do pay to avoid a lawsuit
steps.stepSummary: רבא accepts the claimant's explanation. People often pay to avoid going to court.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: A person often pays to avoid a lawsuit.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא rules on the case. The claimant's explanation is believed, so his offer to buy does not cost him his land.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An offer to buy is not automatic proof that the buyer admits the seller owns it. Paying to avoid a court fight is a normal thing people do.

keyTerms.meaning: רבא, the אמורא who rules in these cases
A person tends to, it is normal for people

steps.whatToRemember: Offering to buy land is not an admission that it belongs to the other person. People pay just to avoid a court case.

phrases.english: רבא said:
A person tends to buy off his lawsuit.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא: עֲבִיד אִינִישׁ דְּזָבֵין דִּינֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Accepts the claimant's answer from step 12.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The claimant keeps his claim, because paying to avoid a lawsuit is normal and is not an admission.

steps.title: Another case: bought and held for the years of חזקה
steps.stepSummary: Again a man challenges someone holding his land. The holder says he bought it from a certain person and used it for the years of חזקה.
steps.simpleTranslation: A man said to another: Why are you on this land? He answered: I bought it from so-and-so and used it for the years of חזקה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins another new case, the last one in this amud. It opens with the same words as the last one, and sets up the next challenge.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The holder says he used the land for 'שני חזקה'. Normally that means three years, the usual time needed for חזקה. This detail becomes the key point of the case.

keyTerms.meaning: And I used it, ate its produce

phrases.english: There was a certain person who said to another:
What are you doing with this land?
He said to him: I bought it from so-and-so,
and I used it for the years of חזקה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new, separate case, again ruled on by רבא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Sets up the case: the holder claims purchase plus use for the years of חזקה.

steps.title: The claimant's document: I bought it from him four years ago
steps.stepSummary: The claimant shows a document that he bought the land from that same seller four years ago. So if the holder bought it only three years ago, the seller no longer owned it.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said: But I hold a document that I bought it from him four years ago!
steps.whatsHappening: The claimant challenges the holder's purchase. He says he bought the land from the same seller first.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The claimant understands 'שני חזקה' as three years. If his purchase was four years ago, it came first, and the seller had nothing left to sell the holder.

keyTerms.meaning: A document, here a bill of sale

phrases.english: He said to him: But I am holding a document
that I bought it from him
phrases.notes: "Him" is the same seller the holder says he bought from.

phrases.english: already four years ago!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the holder's claim of purchase and חזקה.
steps.kashyaTarget: The holder's claim that he bought the land and owns it.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the holder bought it three years ago and the claimant bought it four years ago, the claimant's purchase came first.

steps.title: The holder: by 'years of חזקה' I meant many years
steps.stepSummary: The holder explains that he did not mean exactly three years. He meant he held the land for many years, more than four.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said: Do you think that by 'years of חזקה' I meant three years? I meant many years of חזקה.
steps.whatsHappening: The holder answers the claimant. His purchase was earlier than the claimant's four years.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The claimant took 'שני חזקה' to mean exactly three years. The holder says he used the phrase loosely for a long time. If so, his purchase came first and he owns the land.

phrases.english: He said to him: Do you think that by "years of חזקה"
I was saying three years?!
I was saying many years of חזקה.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִי סָבְרַתְּ שְׁנֵי חֲזָקָה תְּלָת שְׁנֵי קָא אָמֵינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the claimant's document by explaining what 'שני חזקה' meant.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Re-reading the words of the claim
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'שני חזקה' meant exactly three years, so the claimant's four-year-old purchase came first.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'שני חזקה' meant many years, so the holder's purchase came first.

steps.title: רבא: people call many years 'years of חזקה'
steps.stepSummary: רבא accepts the holder's explanation. People commonly use 'שני חזקה' to mean many years.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: People often call many years 'years of חזקה'.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא rules on the case. The holder's explanation is believed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase 'שני חזקה' is not read as an exact count of three years. Since people use it loosely, the holder's words do not trap him into a date after the claimant's purchase.
steps.whatToRemember: רבא's last two rulings follow how people really talk and act. Offering to buy is not an admission, and 'שני חזקה' can mean many years, not exactly three.

phrases.english: רבא said: People commonly
call many years "years of חזקה".

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא: עֲבִידִי אִינָשֵׁי דְּקָרוּ לִשְׁנֵי טוּבָא שְׁנֵי חֲזָקָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Accepts the holder's answer from step 16.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The holder's claim is accepted, because 'שני חזקה' is commonly used to mean many years.

steps.title: The holder wins only if he used the land for seven years
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא limits רבא's ruling. The holder wins only if he used the land for seven years, so his חזקה was complete before the claimant's שטר was written.
steps.simpleTranslation: This ruling applies only when he used the land for seven years. That way, this holder's חזקה came before that claimant's שטר.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא puts a limit on רבא's ruling from the last step. The holder's 'many years' explanation only wins if he actually used the land for seven years.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The claimant's שטר is four years old. A חזקה takes three years. So the holder needs 4 + 3 = 7 years: three full years of use before the claimant's purchase, and the four years since then. If he has that, his חזקה was already complete before the claimant bought the land. That means the seller no longer owned it to sell to the claimant.

keyTerms.meaning: 'And these words apply only…' A phrase that limits an earlier ruling.
He 'ate' it, meaning he used the land and took its produce.
A document. Here, the claimant's bill of sale.
A proven ownership claim, built by using land for three years.

steps.whatToRemember: Saying 'many years' is not enough by itself. The holder must have used the land for seven years, so his three-year חזקה was finished before the claimant's four-year-old שטר.
steps.confusionAlert: 'Seven' is not a new length for חזקה. It is still three years. The extra four years just cover the time since the claimant's שטר was written.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows how a שטר and a חזקה compete: whichever came first in time decides who owns the land.

phrases.english: And this applies only if he used the land for seven years
so that this one's חזקה came before that one's document
phrases.notes: 'This one' is the person holding the land; 'that one' is the claimant with the four-year-old שטר.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Qualifies רבא's acceptance of the holder's explanation in Step 17.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The holder wins only if he used the land for seven years, so his three-year חזקה was complete before the claimant's four-year-old שטר.
